data.name: Eric
data.long_meaning: Eric originated from Old Norse 'Eirikr', which means 'ruler, powerful one'. It was also adopted from Hebrew 'Ezra', meaning 'help'. In Scandinavian folklore, Eric the Red discovered Iceland. In Christian tradition, St. Eric, also known as St. Eskil or St. Isiglindis, was a bishop in Sweden. He is known for his efforts to spread Christianity and is celebrated as a patron saint for travellers.

data.spiritual_significance: Eric's name holds a rich spiritual significance as it was linked to both Norse and Christian traditions. It carried the meaning of a powerful ruler, while also alluding to the Christian saint who dedicated his life to spreading the message of Christianity. This name would have resonated with those who admired power and strength but also valued spiritual growth and enlightenment.

historical_references.reference: Saint Eric the Ever-reading, also known as Saint Eric of Västergås, was a Christian monk and bishop in Sweden during the late 11th century. He is best known for his dedication to reading and study, which earned him the epithet 'Ever-reading'. According to legend, he carried a large book with him wherever he went, even during his travels on foot. He is said to have spent most of his time in seclusion, reading and praying in a cave near present-day Eriksberg, Sweden. He is sometimes considered the patron saint of students and scholars.

Eric the Victorious, also known as Saint Eric or King Eric IX of Sweden, was a Christian king of Sweden from 1156 to 1160. He is remembered for his victories against the pagan Wends and Estonians, which helped to spread Christianity throughout Sweden and the Baltic region. Eric was also known for his piety and his commitment to the welfare of his people.
